articles.title: In 2015, Canada sank a 113-metre retired warship off British Columbia; five years later, monitoring had recorded more than 170 marine species on the wreck
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: A retired Canadian warship that was deliberately sunk off British Columbia in 2015 has become an artificial reef supporting a growing community of mar.
articles.body: A retired Canadian warship that was deliberately sunk off British Columbia in 2015 has become an artificial reef supporting a growing community of marine life. The former HMCS Annapolis, measuring 113.1 metres in length, was placed on the seabed at Halkett Bay Marine Park near Gambier Island to create additional habitat in an area affected by decades of log-boom storage. According to the Artificial Reef Society of British Columbia (ARSBC), five years of biodiversity monitoring eventually documented more than 170 species of marine flora and fauna living on the wreck. Canada's Environment and Climate Change Canada records confirm that the vessel was approved for disposal at sea under a permit issued under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.From warship to reefThe Annapolis was a former Canadian naval destroyer escort that had been decommissioned before eventually being acquired by the Artificial Reef Society of British Columbia. After extensive preparation and environmental cleanup, the 113.1-metre vessel was sunk on April 4, 2015, at Halkett Bay Marine Park. The ship was placed in about 32 metres of water, creating a large vertical and horizontal structure on what had previously been a relatively flat seabed.The Canadian government's disposal-at-sea permit specified that the ship had to be cleared of materials that could create floating debris or marine pollution. Petroleum-based products, including fuel oil, hydraulic fluids and lubricants, had to be removed before the vessel was disposed of. The permit also required the ship to meet Environment Canada's cleanup standards before sinking. The vessel was ultimately scuttled using explosive cutting, which allowed water to enter the hull and send the ship to the seabed.Life arrived quicklyThe wreck did not remain an empty structure for long. The ARSBC established the Annapolis Biodiversity Index Study, or ABIS, to document how marine organisms gradually colonised the ship. The monitoring initially relied on observations and photographs submitted by recreational divers. From 2016, a dedicated group of citizen-science divers began collecting observations more consistently, allowing researchers and marine taxonomists to track changes in the biological community over time. By early 2016, nearly 50 marine species had already been recorded on the Annapolis. Over the following years, the list continued to expand as organisms occupied different parts of the ship and established themselves on its surfaces.More than 170 speciesBy the time the ABIS report was published in June 2021, the taxonomic record for the wreck had grown to more than 170 species of marine flora and fauna. The ARSBC reported that representatives of all marine phyla found in British Columbia waters were present on the Annapolis. The five-year monitoring period also documented several rockfish species, including juveniles. These observations were significant because the artificial reef had been created partly to provide additional habitat for rockfish and lingcod, populations of which had experienced declines in Howe Sound. The monitoring also recorded lingcod egg masses on the ship. Lingcod guarding eggs is one of the signs that the wreck is providing more than a temporary surface for marine organisms; it can also support important stages of reproduction.A changing underwater ecosystemAn artificial reef does not instantly become a mature ecosystem. Instead, colonisation happens gradually as organisms find surfaces on which to attach, shelter and feed. The ABIS observations followed this progression on the Annapolis. Early growth included microbial and algal films, followed by invertebrates and increasingly diverse fish communities. As organisms established themselves, they also created new habitat for other species.The ship's complex structure provides both exposed surfaces and sheltered spaces that are difficult to find on a relatively featureless seabed. That physical complexity can help create niches for organisms with different habitat requirements. The ARSBC has continued to receive observations from divers even after the formal ABIS programme ended. Its reports note that new species can continue to appear and existing populations can increase as the artificial reef matures.What the wreck showsThe Annapolis project provides a long-term example of how a carefully prepared artificial structure can become part of a marine ecosystem. It also demonstrates the value of monitoring such projects rather than judging their ecological effects immediately after installation. The more than 170 species recorded on the wreck do not, by themselves, mean that the artificial reef has restored the broader Howe Sound ecosystem. The ARSBC itself notes that rockfish and lingcod numbers remain depressed across Howe Sound. Instead, the observations show that the Annapolis has developed into a substantial habitat for marine life at its specific location.What began as the final resting place of a retired warship has therefore become something very different beneath the surface: a large artificial habitat whose biological community has continued to develop year after year.

articles.title: Human hair, receipts, fishing nets, and eggshells were among 17 waste materials tested to create stronger, lower-carbon cement building products
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: Cement is one of the most widely used materials in construction, but its production comes with a high environmental cost. Circular Design Cement, a 20.
articles.body: Cement is one of the most widely used materials in construction, but its production comes with a high environmental cost. Circular Design Cement, a 2026 James Dyson Award project, is exploring a new approach to construction materials. The project uses everyday waste and industrial byproducts as recycled aggregates in cement-based materials designed for architectural applications. The work replaces some conventional aggregates with materials such as eggshells, glass, ceramics and oyster shells while using blast furnace slag cement as a lower-carbon binder. These recycled materials can be turned into thin boards, tiles and small architectural products that retain strength, function and visual appeal while using fewer natural resources.How Circular Design Cement turns waste into building materialCircular Design Cement starts with the idea that construction materials do not always need to rely on newly extracted resources. The project uses recycled waste as aggregates and combines them with blast furnace slag cement. Materials are crushed, cut, or separated before being mixed with the binder.The mixture is poured into moulds and shaped through press dewatering, which compacts the material while removing excess water. It is cured naturally or with steam rather than being fired at high temperatures. The approach can produce cement boards, tiles, and architectural products. Testing examined bending strength, impact resistance, and dimensional stability across formulations.How recycled materials are changing the design of cement boardsThe project addresses two major challenges in construction that are the environmental impact of cement production and pressure on resources such as sand and gravel. Circular Design Cement explores thinner cement boards that can reduce material use while providing useful performance. Its inspiration partly came from thick, heavily coated cement boards seen in Japan. The designers explored fibre reinforcement and lower-carbon binders to develop a different approach to these products. The project also draws inspiration from early reinforced cement innovations associated with Joseph Monier. By combining a thinner form with recycled inputs, it aims to make construction materials more efficient without losing practical qualities.17 waste materials tested for stronger building tilesThe design process tested 17 waste materials in 7.5-centimetre tiles. The materials included glass, ceramics, wood chips, denim fibres, hair, eggshells, oyster shells, ocean plastics, fishing nets, receipts and iron oxide from disposable hand warmers. Different mixture ratios revealed possibilities and limitations. Wood-chip mixtures retained too much water, while eggshell-based mixtures presented other challenges. Hair was found to be incompatible with the alkaline cement environment. After this testing, eggshells, ceramics, glass, oyster shells, and iron oxide were selected for validation. The team then refined the mixing, pressing, and curing process before comparing materials with conventional cement boards through mechanical tests.How recycled materials can strengthen cement productsThe selected materials were tested after the manufacturing process. Some formulations recorded bending strengths of up to 16.1 N/mm², exceeding those of conventional cement boards. The material also uses Type B blast furnace slag cement, which has a lower reported carbon emission factor than ordinary Portland cement. The binder can reduce the need for conventional sand after combining with recycled aggregates. The designers also explored the visual possibilities of waste materials, including the textures and colours they could create. A denim-reinforced flowerpot prototype further showed how the approach could be used beyond flat cement boards.Further tests will focus on durability and recyclingThe project is being developed, with next steps focused on making the material more reliable and practical. The team plans to carry out further testing, including assessments of fire and water resistance. It also aims to scale the work from small prototypes to full-size boards while refining the life cycle assessment. As production grows, securing a consistent supply of suitable waste materials will become important. The team also plans to explore whether the products can be recycled after use. The project ultimately brings waste recovery and lower-impact construction together through a single material approach.

articles.title: Dutch scientists pipe office urine into bacteria-filled cells that generate electricity and recover nitrogen and phosphorus, while a related system can produce hydrogen
articles.summary: Experiments & Discoveries News: Pee breaks are one of the most relaxing times in the office when you finally get to have some sane moments to yourself. Which is why most employees ta.
articles.body: Pee breaks are one of the most relaxing times in the office when you finally get to have some sane moments to yourself. Which is why most employees take numerous such breaks within a day. But what if your normal pee break had you secretly contributing to the generation of electricity?Two hundred and sixty men walked into an office toilet in the north of the Netherlands and became a very small power station. Their contributions went down a dedicated urinal, out through a pipe and into a shipping container parked beside the building. Water board Friesland had asked its male staff to use that urinal, as reported by Dutch Water Sector.It fed a pilot rig for bio-electrochemical treatment, built by Wetsus, the water technology research centre in Leeuwarden. The rig pulled phosphate out of the stream, captured ammonia and generated electricity. Wetsus said the output was enough to run the water board's electric cars about 50km a day.How bacteria turn urine into currentBacteria make their living by breaking down organic matter, which means stripping electrons off it and handing them to something else, normally oxygen. Take the oxygen away, put a carbon electrode in front of them, and they hand those electrons to it instead. Wire that to a second electrode across a membrane and the electrons travel the long way round, through the wire. Current, produced by microbes doing what microbes already do. No turbine, no combustion, no moving parts anywhere in the box.Urine happens to be excellent bacteria food: salty, conductive, and loaded with urea. Writing in Trends in Biotechnology, Pablo Ledezma and co-authors from the University of Queensland and Wetsus made the case that separately collected urine is an unusually promising feedstock for these systems, precisely because it hasn’t yet been diluted into the general wastewater stream.A fertiliser is worth more than the wattsA fact sheet from Eawag, the Swiss aquatic research institute, attributes 85 to 90% of all nitrogen in domestic wastewater to urine alone. Phosphorus runs 50 to 80 per cent, potassium 80 to 90. Every bit of that arrives inside well under one per cent of the total volume.Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium: the three numbers printed on every bag of fertiliser. Sewage plants currently spend energy aerating tanks to destroy that nitrogen, while fertiliser plants burn gas to manufacture more of it somewhere else. Catching it at the toilet skips both errands.In a paper published in Water Research, Philipp Kuntke and colleagues ran real undiluted urine through an air-cathode cell and recovered ammonium at 3.29 grams of nitrogen per square metre of membrane per day. The energy balance came out with a surplus of 3.46 kilojoules per gram of nitrogen, meaning the cell made more electricity than the recovery step spent.A related reactor makes hydrogenIn both devices, bacteria clinging to the anode break down organic matter and hand off electrons the same way. What differs is the cathode. In a fuel cell, those electrons meet oxygen there and current flows out on its own. In the hydrogen version, properly called a microbial electrolysis cell, the cathode is kept oxygen-free and wired for a different job: protons pick up electrons and become hydrogen gas, bubbling off to be collected. That reaction needs a push from outside, a small voltage fed in on top of what the bacteria supply, because the anode’s own electron flow can’t quite force it through alone.Kuntke’s group reported in the International Journal of Hydrogen Energy that five-times-diluted urine in a microbial electrolysis cell produced hydrogen at 48.6 cubic metres per cubic metre of reactor per day, while stripping out ammonium and organic load at high rates.Sadly, the output is humbling. Field trials run by the University of the West of England and documented in Environmental Science: Water Research & Technology had a campus urinal wired with 288 fuel cells averaging 75 milliwatts, and a Glastonbury Festival version with 432 cells averaging 300. Plenty for lights inside a cubicle. Nowhere near a kettle. That Glastonbury unit was handling roughly a thousand users a day, which gives some sense of how much biology it takes to keep a light on.Ammonia drifting back across the membrane cut short the stable operating window in the hydrogen work. Kuntke’s team later moved to a hydrogen gas recycling design, published in ACS Sustainable Chemistry & Engineering, aiming to get ammonia recovery working at a larger scale with less energy. A 2020 review in ChemElectroChem traced the whole field back to three papers published independently in 2012, in Britain, the Netherlands and China, and found most of what followed still stuck at proof of concept

articles.title: Meet Franklin Howley-Dumit Serulle, the amateur naturalist whose online insect photo helped reveal a new hoverfly species
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: A photograph shared online has helped scientists identify a hoverfly species that had remained a mystery for years. The insect, named ‘Monoceromyia nd.
articles.body: A photograph shared online has helped scientists identify a hoverfly species that had remained a mystery for years. The insect, named ‘Monoceromyia ndidiae’, was photographed in the Dominican Republic and posted on iNaturalist. Its unusual appearance caught the attention of an entomologist, who began asking whether the fly represented something unknown.The mystery was finally solved when researchers found a corresponding specimen during a field expedition to Valle Nuevo National Park. Laboratory work at the University of Lausanne confirmed that it was an undescribed species. According to the Swiss Academy of Sciences (SCNAT), the discovery has earned the Swiss Systematics Society’s New Species of the Year 2026 title, highlighting how amateur observations can help reveal biodiversity.How Franklin Howley-Dumit Serulle’s photograph helped scientists discover a new hoverflyFranklin Howley-Dumit Serulle is an amateur naturalist whose interest in insects led him to photograph the unusual hoverfly in the Dominican Republic. He shared the photograph on iNaturalist, where it caught the attention of researchers because the insect could not be identified with certainty. Serulle’s observation became an important starting point in the search for its identity. Although he was not working as part of the research team, his photograph preserved a record of the unusual insect and helped bring it to the attention of specialists. Researchers later found a specimen during fieldwork, allowing them to examine the insect and establish that it was a new species.How researchers confirmed the new hoverfly species in the Dominican RepublicThe discovery took researchers to Valle Nuevo National Park in the Dominican Republic. During a field expedition, they used a light trap and captured a specimen that appeared to be the insect from the online photograph. The specimen allowed scientists to examine its features closely and carry out further laboratory tests.Researchers at the University of Lausanne examined the specimen and confirmed that it belonged to a species previously unknown to science. The insect was formally described as Monoceromyia ndidiae. Its discovery brought together the original photograph shared by an amateur naturalist and the specimen collected during fieldwork. The photograph first drew attention to the unusual insect, while the specimen gave researchers the chance to study it in detail.What makes ‘Monoceromyia ndidiae’ different from other hoverfliesMonoceromyia ndidiae belongs to the hoverfly family, a group known for an unusual form of protection. Many hoverflies have yellow or orange patterns that make them resemble wasps. The resemblance helps protect them from predators even though hoverflies are harmless and cannot sting. This striking appearance may be one reason hoverflies often catch people’s attention. It also gives scientists a better understanding of the biodiversity in the Dominican Republic. The discovery adds another species to the region’s biodiversity records and gives researchers a clearer picture of the hoverflies found there.Why hoverflies matter to ecosystems and biodiversityThe larvae of many hoverfly species feed on aphids, while adult hoverflies help pollinate plants. Their presence can also give researchers clues about the health of an ecosystem and changes taking place in a habitat. About 500 hoverfly species are known in Switzerland, showing the wide variety within this group.SCNAT notes that nearly eight million plant, fungal and animal species may still be unknown to science. Amateur naturalists often discover unusual insects and share their photographs online, giving scientists a chance to notice species that might otherwise be overlooked.

articles.title: Britain’s turtle doves lost 98% of their population since the 1960s; in 2026, conservationists released 30 birds and one began laying eggs
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: As the festive season approaches, a bird forever linked with love, devotion and Christmas is quietly offering Britain a reason for hope. The turtle do.
articles.body: As the festive season approaches, a bird forever linked with love, devotion and Christmas is quietly offering Britain a reason for hope. The turtle dove, once a familiar sight across the countryside, has suffered a dramatic decline over the past six decades. Now, a conservation effort in Hampshire is showing early signs that the species may have a chance to recover, reports People. A recent report by the BBC states that by 2023, the European turtle dove population in the United Kingdom had fallen to just 2 percent of its peak population in the late 1960s. The species is Europe's only migratory dove and has become the fastest-declining bird species in the U.K., adds the report.30 birds take lightIf we go by the People report, in spring 2026, the country's National Park Authority released 30 turtle doves at an undisclosed location in Hampshire. The initiative was designed to strengthen the dwindling population and give the species a better chance of establishing itself in the region. The effort is already producing an encouraging development. South Downs National Park has reported that at least one of the released females has returned to an enclosure and laid eggs, adds the report.For conservationists, the discovery is an important early indication that the birds are adapting successfully. If the released turtle doves continue to thrive, they are expected to make an extraordinary journey of around 3,000 miles to sub-Saharan Africa for the winter before returning to Britain in spring.Creating a home for turtle dovesThe release of the birds is only one part of the wider conservation programme. South Downs National Park, farmers, landowners, volunteers and conservation groups have been working together to improve the habitat available to turtle doves. The report adds that new ponds and areas of scrub have been created across the park and surrounding countryside. Plants that provide food for the birds have also been encouraged, while woodland edges, hedgerows and farmland are being managed to create the conditions turtle doves need.These changes are particularly important because the species depends on a mixture of farmland, scrub, hedgerows and woodland habitats, often with ponds nearby.Looking beyond 30 birdsConservationists are cautiously optimistic, but they know that rebuilding the population will take time. The current project is not relying solely on the 30 birds released in 2026. A further 100 turtle doves are scheduled to be released in spring 2027, clarifies the report by People.Meanwhile, members of the public are helping conservationists track the released birds by reporting sightings. These observations allow researchers to monitor their movements and better understand how the birds are settling into their new surroundings. The discovery of eggs is especially encouraging because successful breeding could help create a self-sustaining population.A Christmas story with a different endingFor generations, turtle doves have been immortalised by their appearance in The 12 Days of Christmas. Yet their real-life story has been far less joyful, marked by decades of population decline. The first eggs produced by a released bird in Hampshire offer a small but meaningful reversal of that story. With improved habitats, continued monitoring and more birds joining the programme, conservationists hope the turtle dove can once again become a familiar presence in Britain's countryside. For a species that has come so close to disappearing, even a single nest can represent the beginning of something much bigger.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: From 2012 to 2022, nearly 30,000 commercial vessel arrivals brought 430 sq km of submerged hull surface to Alaska; biofouling habitat grew 50%, increasing invasive-species risk
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: The submerged surfaces of nearly 30,000 commercial vessels arriving in Alaska over 11 years created more opportunities for marine organisms to hitchhi.
articles.body: The submerged surfaces of nearly 30,000 commercial vessels arriving in Alaska over 11 years created more opportunities for marine organisms to hitchhike to new locations, according to a research.The study, published in Frontiers in Marine Science, examined 29,799 commercial vessel arrivals to Alaskan ports over the 11-year period, Frontiers Media SA reported. It looked at six major vessel types inlcuding bulkers, container ships, general cargo ships, passenger vessels, tankers and roll-on-roll-off (RoRo) vessels, to assess their potential role in transporting non-indigenous species through biofouling.Biofouling happens when marine organisms attach to or occupy submerged parts of a vessel. These can include fixed organisms such as tunicates, bivalves, sponges, bryozoans and algae, as well as mobile organisms. Some of these species can become marine invaders if they survive transport and establish themselves in a new environment.The researchers found that overall vessel arrivals to Alaska increased 23% during the study period. However, the wetted surface area increased faster, rising from 39.9 sq km in 2012 to 59.7 sq km in 2022 which was a 50% increase. The rise was mainly driven by growing traffic from large passenger vessels.Passenger vessels introducing more marine NISPassenger vessels made up the largest share of arrivals during the study period, with 15,984 arrivals in total. They were followed by tankers, with 6,481 arrivals, and container ships, with 3,808 arrivals.The size of the vessels was important because larger vessels provide more submerged surface where biofouling organisms can grow. Passenger vessels had the highest mean WSA per arrival at 17,658 sq m. Tankers followed with 13,503 sq m, while bulkers had an average of 10,066 sq m.Passenger vessels also accounted for more than half of the total WSA arriving in Alaska. They contributed an annual average of 25.7 sq km, compared with 8 sq km from tankers and 2.9 sq km from container ships.The researchers found that passenger vessels had the highest relative likelihood of introducing marine non-indigenous species or NIS through biofouling among the vessel types included in the study. Their importance was linked not only to their size, but also to their high number and frequency of arrivals and their connections with environmentally similar locations.Risk varied across AlaskaThe amount and type of vessel traffic differed considerably between Alaska’s coastal regions. The North American Pacific Fjordland region recorded the highest number of arrivals, with 14,951 during the study period. The Gulf of Alaska followed with 11,292 arrivals, while the Aleutian Islands recorded 2,299.Passenger vessels dominated traffic in the North American Pacific Fjordland region, while tankers were the most common vessels in the Gulf of Alaska. Container ships dominated arrivals to the Aleutian Islands, particularly at Dutch Harbor.The North American Pacific Fjordland and Gulf of Alaska regions were identified as having the highest relative risk of marine NIS introduction from hull biofouling. These areas receive large amounts of vessel traffic and have connections with regions where environmental conditions can be relatively similar.More than half of all arrivals came from locations within Alaska. A total of 16,269 arrivals represented 237.6 sq km of WSA. Nearly a third of all arrivals, or 9,368 vessels, came from the North American Pacific coastline, representing 139.6 sq km of WSA.The researchers also examined how similar the environmental conditions were between a vessel's last port of call and its arrival location. Smaller environmental distance indicates greater similarity and potentially better conditions for a transported species to survive.Time in port and dry docking also matterWSA was only one of the factors examined. The researchers also considered environmental distance, the amount of time vessels remained in port and the number of years since their last dry dock.Longer residency time can provide biofouling organisms with more opportunity to reproduce or move into an arrival port. Passenger, RoRo and container vessels had the shortest average residency times, ranging from 0.5 to 1.1 days. General cargo vessels and tankers averaged 3.2 and 3.4 days, respectively, while bulkers had the longest average stay at 5.6 days.The researchers also used years since the last dry dock as an indicator of potential biofouling accumulation. More time since dry docking can be linked to greater accumulation, although the study did not treat this measure as a direct measure of biofouling because dry docking does not always include hull treatment.The risk assessment does not mean that every organism transported on a vessel will become established. The researchers noted that successful establishment depends on both the number of organisms introduced and whether they can survive and reproduce in the new environment.Climate change adds another concernThe study says Alaska faces a changing risk because environmental conditions and shipping patterns are also changing. Warming waters may make parts of the state more suitable for marine NIS that were previously limited by colder conditions.At the same time, reduced sea ice is making Arctic shipping routes more accessible. The researchers noted that vessels travelling through the Arctic must cross the Bering Sea when travelling to or from the Arctic Ocean, potentially increasing traffic through Alaska's subarctic regions.The researchers said the findings can help identify vessels and ports that should receive greater attention for monitoring. They suggested prioritising vessels with larger WSA, longer stays in port, greater environmental similarity with their previous locations or longer periods since dry docking.For Alaska, where ports can be remote and resources for monitoring are limited, the researchers said establishing a baseline of biofouling risk could help direct monitoring and mitigation efforts towards the vessels and locations with the greatest potential for marine NIS introduction.

articles.title: Gray whales are washing up dead on the West Coast. The reason is alarming
articles.summary: In March a whale corpse was found floating in San Francisco Bay, seagulls perched on top like vultures at carrion.  As of mid-August, 187 gray whales have be...
articles.body:
The bodies kept appearing as if out of nowhere. In March a whale corpse was found floating in San Francisco Bay, seagulls perched on top like vultures at carrion. Then, in April, a whale was found dead and beached in Oregon, the arc of its carcass camouflaged against the surf. That same month, another whale, this one a juvenile, was found lifeless and lodged among woody debris in a Washington State river, miles from the ocean.

As of mid-August, 187 gray whales have been found dead this year along the West Coast, from Mexico to Alaska. Scientists have scrambled to investigate, hoping to prevent further deaths in a species that has been in decline for years—gray whales lost 35 percent of their population between 2020 and 2025.

There's been a "complete decline [and] a collapse of reproduction," says Steven Swartz, co-director and senior scientist at the Gray Whale Research in Mexico program. The whale corpses now washing up on the West Coast hold clues as to why: many of them were emaciated, so much so that one scientist described them as "a bag of bones."

It's an incredible and horrifying twist of fate for a whale that had until recently been a major conservation success story. Decimated by whaling in the 19th century, the eastern North Pacific gray whale population had bounced back from near extinction to roughly 20,000 animals by 1994, when the species was removed from the U.S. Endangered Species List. By 2016 the whales numbered some 27,000 individuals. But as of 2025, the population had plummeted to 13,000 or so, as whale after whale washed up on shores up and down the West Coast.

Scientists, meanwhile, have been racing to explain what is happening to the whales by studying the stranded corpses for signs and clues that could illuminate why they are dying in droves.

Gray whales are baleen whales that have mottled skin, a dorsal hump, pointed pectoral fins and eyes set low above permanently frowning mouths. They can reach 49 feet long and weigh up to 90,000 pounds, as much as six large elephants. Each year they make one of the longest known mammal migrations on Earth, a roughly 10,000-mile round trip between Mexico and the Arctic. The whales are seasonal ecosystem engineers, stirring up nutrients on the seafloor as they feed.

The mysterious strandings began in earnest in mid-December 2018. And in 2019 the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) declared an unusual mortality event, triggering an international investigation. Scientists rushed to study the stranded whales, searching for clues. They took the whales' measurements, inspected their bodies for signs of starvation or trauma, cut them open to examine their blubber and took samples from their organs. The analyses pointed to malnutrition as a common cause of death, followed by blunt force trauma consistent with being struck by boats.

In other words, the whales were either dying as a result of a lack of food or because boats had crashed into them.

The unusual mortality event officially ended in 2023 after strandings slowed—but the whales haven't stopped dying. Instead the decline has only become "more alarming," says John Calambokidis, senior research biologist and co-founder of the nonprofit Cascadia Research Collective. Though overall population numbers ticked up slightly this year, to an estimated 18,000, "the overall trend is still a decline," says Aimée Lang, a research scientist with the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Southwest Fisheries Science Center.

As scientists gather more evidence, it is becoming increasingly apparent that gray whales are starving to death. The reason why lies in the changing environment of the Arctic Ocean.

Gray whales are mostly bottom-feeders, scooping up mouthfuls of sediment and invertebrates as they swim along the seafloor. They trap shrimplike amphipods and filter out the muck through baleen plates attached to their upper jaws ⁠ , leaving wallows and billows of mud—a nutrient feast for other organisms—in their wake. This buffet is intricately linked to the Arctic sea ice and the algae that grows beneath it.

When the algae die, they fall through the water column to the seafloor, where they feed the crustaceans that gray whales eat. But with Arctic temperatures skyrocketing, the sea ice is melting earlier and faster, disrupting the food web the whales rely on.

That was the conclusion of a study published late last year in the ICES Journal of Marine Science that examined decades worth of data on the population sizes, births and deaths of gray whales and the biomass of Arctic crustaceans. It turns out that the health of the whales and the crustaceans ebbs and flows in near perfect synchrony, says study co-author Joshua Stewart, an assistant professor at Oregon State University's Marine Mammal Institute. And though gray whale populations have dipped periodically before, this time is different: "We're not seeing signs of the population quickly bouncing back like we did previously," Stewart says. Essentially, the ecosystem can no longer support as many gray whales as it once did. As a result, the whales are starving.

"The whales are just basically running out of energy as they try to migrate and dying," Swartz says. For years, he's seen more and more skinny gray whales returning to the San Ignacio Lagoon, one of their breeding areas off the Baja coast. He is also seeing far fewer calves being born. Lang, who helps count mothers and calves as they migrate north along the California coast, says that last year the team counted just 17 whale pairs. From that, they estimate 85 calves were born in 2025, well below the 1,600 or so born in 2014.

As dire as the situation is, there is still a chance that gray whales can survive this. For one, the animals could adapt to changing conditions in the Arctic by looking for food elsewhere, Lang says. They've "shown pretty amazing behavioral flexibility already," she adds.

Already there is evidence some gray whales are switching it up. A small group of gray whales called the Sounders detour from their northward migration to feed in Puget Sound, and then there is the Pacific Coast Feeding Group, which eschews the Arctic to feed between northern California and British Columbia.

There's other evidence to suggest more whales are joining those alternative routes. Gray whales have also been seen more frequently in San Francisco Bay since 2018, and scientists suspect they're searching for food there, too. But the heavy marine traffic in the Bay makes it a dangerous place for a whale: at least 18 percent of the whales that entered between 2018 and 2025 died there , according to a recent Frontiers in Marine Science study,many of which were killed by ships. A nascent system using AI and thermal cameras could help ships better spot the whales and reduce ship strikes, but it's still being tested.

These efforts also do little to address the core threat to gray whales. "The challenge with this case is that the lever we have to pull is slowing or reversing climate change," Stewart says. "It's something we know we need to do, but we haven't done it."

As the summer turns to fall and gray whales begin their return journey south, scientists will be watching closely to see how many make it back and what condition they're in when they get there.

"The big question in all our minds is just, where's the bottom?" Stewart says. "I hope they turn around soon."

articles.title: Meet Naidely Valeria Vidaurre-Quesada, the scientist who helped uncover a ghost shark species hiding in Costa Rica’s dark waters
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Far below the surface of Costa Rica’s Pacific coast, where sunlight disappears and fishing grounds give way to deep water, three unusual fish specimen.
articles.body: Far below the surface of Costa Rica’s Pacific coast, where sunlight disappears and fishing grounds give way to deep water, three unusual fish specimens had been sitting in scientific collections for years. They would eventually become the basis for describing a species unknown to science. At the centre of that work was Naidely Valeria Vidaurre-Quesada, a biology student at the University of Costa Rica who became the lead author of the study. The fish belonged to the chimaera family, a little-known group of cartilaginous animals related to sharks and rays and often called ghost sharks. The species, named Rhinochimaera costaricana, was formally described in Zootaxa on June 10, 2026.Costa Rica’s deep waters held clues to a new ghost shark speciesAccording to the study published in Zootaxa, titled, ‘A new species of Rhinochimaera Garman 1901 (Holocephali: Chimaeriformes: Rhinochimaeridae) from the Eastern Pacific Ocean’ reveals the first of the three specimens was collected in 2000 near Isla del Caño. Two more were recovered much later, in 2023, during fisheries research off Cabo Blanco in Puntarenas. All three were male, measuring between 775 and 830 millimetres long.Their habitat was far removed from the familiar coastal waters of Costa Rica. The specimens came from depths between 390 and 787 metres, placing them in a part of the Pacific that remains difficult to study directly.For years, individual specimens can exist in collections without their significance being fully understood. In this case, bringing the material together allowed Vidaurre-Quesada and her colleagues to examine whether the fish represented a known species or something that had escaped scientific recognition.Naidely Vidaurre-Quesada: The scientist behind a new ghost shark discoveryNaidely Valeria Vidaurre-Quesada is a biology student and researcher at the University of Costa Rica. She was the lead author of the scientific study that formally described Rhinochimaera costaricana, a previously unrecognised deep-sea ghost shark from Costa Rica’s Pacific waters.As reported by The Costa Rican News ,as part of the research, she travelled to the Natural History Museum in London, where she examined older specimens and records of the Rhinochimaera genus. This helped the team determine that the Costa Rican specimens were distinct from the three species already known.Her work shows how museum collections, fisheries research and modern genetic analysis can come together to reveal species that have remained scientifically overlooked for years.DNA evidence revealed the fish was unlike the three known speciesThe Rhinochimaera genus already contained three recognised species: R. africana, R. atlantica and R. pacifica. Establishing a fourth required the Costa Rican specimens to be compared with those existing species.DNA sequences provided another line of evidence. The specimens showed genetic differences of 3.9% from R. africana, 4.5% from R. atlantica and 4.7% from R. pacifica.Taken alongside the anatomical characteristics, those differences supported the conclusion that the Costa Rican fish was not simply a regional form of one of the existing species.The scientific name reflects its origin. Rhinochimaera costaricana places the animal within its genus while identifying Costa Rica in its species name.Old museum specimens helped Vidaurre-Quesada confirm a new speciesMuseum collections can provide a useful second look at discoveries like this. A specimen that appears unusual in one collection may turn out to resemble an animal preserved decades earlier somewhere else. Comparing historical material helps researchers avoid giving a new name to something that has already been documented.In Vidaurre-Quesada's case, the work helped establish that the Costa Rican specimens represented a species distinct from the three Rhinochimaera species already recognised.How fisheries research helped uncover the sharkThe discovery also says something about where scientific knowledge can come from. Two of the specimens were obtained during fisheries research rather than a dedicated search for a previously unknown chimaera.That connection between fisheries work and zoological collections gave researchers access to animals from depths that are difficult to reach and observe routinely. Once transferred to the UCR Museum of Zoology, the specimens could be examined, compared and preserved for future work.The collaboration stretched beyond Costa Rica as well. The UCR and Incopesca worked with researchers at the Federal University of Pará in Brazil, while the examination of historical material took Vidaurre-Quesada to the Natural History Museum in London.

articles.title: Besxar is building an orbital semiconductor factory, one SpaceX rocket at a time | TechCrunch
articles.summary: If you want to manufacture in space—and bring the products back again—there's a limited set of options: Wait to go to the International Space Station, or
articles.body:
If you want to manufacture in space—and bring the products back again—there’s a limited set of options: Wait to go to the International Space Station, or partner with a handful of start-ups launching spacecraft that spend time in orbit before they return to Earth.

But the vehicle that goes to space and comes back to Earth more often than any other is a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket booster, which made that round-trip 163 times last year and has already flown more than 100 times this year. Now, a startup says it has talked Elon Musk’s space company into letting it prototype an orbital semiconductor factory across a dozen flights with the booster.

Besxar, a start-up founded by former OpenAI staffer Ashley Pilipiszyn, wants to make the key precursors for advanced semiconductors by taking advantage of the vacuum of space. A key reason chip fabs on Earth are such hugely insane infrastructure projects is the need to create pressurized clean rooms to keep out even microscopic dust and contaminants that could ruin a chip during production. Pilipiszyn argues that a new generation of rockets could offer an alternative to all that infrastructure and to do it, she has raised almost $14 million, including a $9 million seed round led by Dauntless Ventures and Overture VC.

“We’re at a time where it’s actually more cost-effective to go where the physics already works,” she told TechCrunch. “Don’t do it on Earth where you’re fighting physics.”

The company’s first two “fabships”—small canisters designed to carry and test semiconductor materials in orbit—flew on a July Starlink mission and were intended to prove that the canisters could survive a launch, protect wafer samples from contamination, and expose them to the vacuum of space. Besxar succeeded in these objectives despite a malfunction in the flight data system in one canister, which the company is currently investigating.

“The flown samples were the cleanest and had the least amount of particulate matter compared to … non-flown terrestrial wafers, which is fantastic for us as we scale up,” Pilipiszyn told TechCrunch.

Besxar expects to keep iterating over the next two years, with the ultimate goal of flying larger fabs onboard a vehicle like SpaceX’s Starship, the company’s next-generation rocket still in development. Pilipiszyn first approached SpaceX three years ago to talk about buying flights on Starship and eventually settled on the booster payload deal as a way to de-risk her technology in the meantime. Next up is heating the wafers, then depositing one material on the wafers, then two materials, and so forth.

Once it is producing qualification samples, Besxar—named after “beskar,” the metal used in Star Wars to make Mandalorian armor—wants to supply leading chipmakers with the wafers used to make the kinds of advanced chips that regulate electrical power in data centers, robots and electric vehicles.

There are a number of companies working to leverage the space environment for higher-quality semiconductors, including United Semiconductors and Space Forge, but all face the same difficulty: the limited ability to return a meaningful volume of product. Pilipiszyn expects to start to scale up to hundreds and then thousands of wafers per fab, but that path depends on cheap rockets. That in turn requires SpaceX to get Starship operational—or competitors like Rocket Lab and Stoke Space getting their own next-generation rockets off the ground.

“We believe that there is a solid transport layer now, so we can focus on the application layer,” she told TechCrunch. “We can just focus on our core manufacturing and getting our products back down to earth to market as quickly as possible.”

articles.title: Giant Helios sun installation to light up Goole Market Hall
articles.summary: Helios, created by artist Luke Jerram, will be displayed at Goole Market Hall from 25 September.
articles.body:
A large art installation respresenting the sun will light up an East Yorkshire market hall.

Helios, which was created by artist Luke Jerram, will be displayed at Goole Market Hall from 25 September to 5 October.

The touring artwork, named after the ancient Greek mythological god who personified the sun, was made using more than 400,000 high-resolution photographs of the sun's surface and observational data from Nasa.

Councillor Nick Coultish, East Riding of Yorkshire Council's cabinet member for culture, leisure and tourism, said: "We're absolutely delighted to be bringing Helios to Goole Market Hall as part of the Goole 200 programme of events planned to mark our town's bicentenary year."

"I can't think of a more fitting setting than the newly refurbished Market Hall, where this internationally renowned artwork will become a magnificent focal point," he added.

"Helios has attracted huge crowds on its tour of the UK, so is sure to bring a stream of visitors into the town centre during its visit to Goole."

The installation measures 19ft (6m) in diameter and is internally lit.

The visit has been secured with the help of funding from Arts Council England.

The Goole 2026 Bicentenary Group , made up of East Riding of Yorkshire Council and community partners, has planned a programme of Around the Sun events during the time Helios is on display.

It includes an inflatable dome at Junction Goole, which will allow people to explore the solar system, and a concert bringing together classical music and electronic sounds using recordings from NASA.

The artwork can be seen during Goole Market Hall's opening hours.

articles.title: Fossilized eggs of the largest known dinosaurs have been unearthed in an unexpected place
articles.summary: A trove of fossilized eggs reveals that the largest dinosaurs to walk Earth could reproduce far from ideal nesting areas.
articles.body:
The largest dinosaurs that ever lived were able to reproduce at high latitudes — or regions far from the equator — and came up with a clever strategy to keep their eggs warm, a study of a trove of titanosaur eggs unearthed in Argentina has revealed.

Most titanosaur eggs and eggshells, like those of other dinosaurs, have been found in lower-latitude regions closer to the equator, where warmer temperatures would have made incubating the eggs easier.

Scientists think these long-necked, small-brained, plant-eating giants — part of a group known as sauropods — lived in herds and may have migrated over long distances, nesting in the same place for millennia.

"We know their bones have turned up in places as far south as Antarctica and southern Argentina, and as far north as Mongolia and Texas," said Darla Zelenitsky, a paleontologist and associate professor at the University of Calgary in Alberta. Zelenitsky is a senior author of the new research, which published Tuesday in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

"They clearly spent time in higher latitude areas, but until now it wasn't known whether they were also nesting there," Zelenitsky added.

Unlike some smaller dinosaur species and birds today, paleontologists are pretty certain titanosaurs did not brood their own eggs. Their huge size "would have turned the nest into one giant omelette," Zelenitsky said via email.

As such, it's doubtful that titanosaurs were doting parents. Like most reptiles, they likely laid their eggs and left any resulting offspring to fend for themselves.

Eggs, however, need warmth to develop and hatch, and sunlight is in shorter supply at higher latitudes. The study suggests that titanosaurs found a way to deal with lower temperatures in the planet's southernmost reaches although the climate in the late Cretaceous at that latitude would not have been as cool as today's.

"The most likely scenario is that these titanosaurs laid their eggs in mound nests made of vegetation and soil, where incubation heat came mostly from rotting plant material," Zelenitsky said.

"Their eggshells were very porous, which means if the eggs were left out in the open, they would lose water, dry out, and the embryos would die. Buried in sand, soil, or vegetation, the nest would stay humid or damp enough for the eggs to survive," she added.

Researchers discovered the 255 eggshell fragments in the Chorrillo Formation in southern Argentina 200 miles (322 kilometers) north of the Strait of Magellan — the sea route at the southern tip of South America — in 2020 and 2024. They date back 68 million years, when they would have been at latitudes between 55 degrees and 60 degrees south. The clutches of eggs represent the highest-latitude nesting environment known for sauropods worldwide, the study said, and the southernmost definitive evidence of dinosaur eggs.

"What is particularly important about this new discovery, though, is that these dinosaur eggs belonged to titanosaurs, giant potbellied long-necked dinosaurs," said Steve Brusatte, a professor of paleontology and evolution at the University of Edinburgh. He wasn't involved in the research.

"Some of the very largest animals in Earth's history were laying eggs and hatching their babies at high latitudes in the Cretaceous, which is a new fact about dinosaur biology and behaviour that makes us better appreciate their adaptability and resiliency."

Paul Upchurch, a professor of paleobiology at University College London said that sauropod remains are rare at high latitudes and it had been thought that the giants moved to these areas during warm summers before returning closer to the equator.

"Now that we have eggs from a high latitude, this suggests that they might have stayed there all year, or at least were able to go through their reproductive cycle during the warm part of the year at those high latitudes," Upchurch, who also wasn't part of the research team, added.

Titanosaurs include the largest known dinosaurs, with individuals estimated to weigh up to around 75,000 kilograms (more than eight times bigger than a Tyrannosaurus rex). Dinosaur eggs are rare in the fossil record because the eggshell is relatively thin and fragile, and it breaks down quickly into tiny pieces and is difficult to preserve.

It's not clear to which species of titanosaur the eggs belonged, but teeth found at the same site were those of colossosaurian dinosaurs, some of the biggest titanosaurs although not the largest.

"If these eggshells belong to colossosaurians, the hatchlings had to have had plenty of nutritious food resources in that environment to start packing on the tonnes to eventually reach their colossal body sizes," Zelenitsky said.

Even though these dinos were huge, their eggs were tiny — about 1/18,000 the size of the adult dinosaur— and could have contained about 4 liters of liquid, with hatchlings weighing around 4 kilograms (about 9 pounds).

Nonetheless, the titanosaur nests would have been large enough to make a distinct impression on the landscape, especially if the dinosaurs nested communally.

"I envision the nest as a picnic table size mound of dirt and vegetation with the egg clutch buried inside … so it probably wasn't an inconspicuous structure," Zelenitsky said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: Dónde no se podrá vivir en España dentro de 30 años, según la NASA
articles.standfirst: El informa 'Too Hot to Handle: How Climate Change May Make Some Places Too Hot to Live’ da las claves del cambio climático, lo que ocurre en el planeta y pone fechas
articles.summary: El informa 'Too Hot to Handle: How Climate Change May Make Some Places Too Hot to Live’ da las claves del cambio climático, lo que ocurre en el planeta y pone fechas
articles.body: El cambio de tiempo es una realidad en la que los científicos están centrados en los últimos años y en la NASA han dejado una sentencia en alusión al mundo que deja cuanto menos un poso de preocupación al respecto. Desde dicho ente hablan de zonas en España que no serán habitables en apenas 30 años. Evidentemente hay una serie de efectos que provoca el ser humano en una serie de elementos que son determinantes para que se haya llegado a dicha conclusión... El cambio climático está siendo tan intenso y sus consecuencias pueden ser terribles. El aumento de la temperatura del planeta es una realidad que puede acabar siendo la que nos acompañe a partir de ahora y que se ha visto acentuada en este tiempo veraniego donde, por ejemplo, en España se han vivido noches tropicales que han marcado registros récord. Los expertos de la NASA lanzaron hace unos años un informe bajo el título 'Too Hot to Handle: How Climate Change May Make Some Places Too Hot to Live’ en el que advertían de lo que sucedería en 2050. Y vamos acercándonos a esa fecha que puede acabar siguiendo una serie de predicciones que parece que se cumplen por momentos. Se centra en las llamadas olas de calor que ya están empezando a causar estragos por ejemplo en España. Y las zonas de nuestro territorio más amenazadas son Madrid, la Comunidad Valenciana y Andalucía. El dato global es aterrador. Los expertos advierten. "Las olas de calor del pasado ofrecen una visión del futuro para las ciudades que esperan un aumento de las temperaturas. Hoy en día, casi un tercio de la población mundial está expuesta a extremos de calor potencialmente mortales durante 20 días al año o más. Fenómenos como la ola de calor de 2003 en Europa, que se cobró más de 70.000 vidas, serán más frecuentes y graves a partir de la década de 2040". El informe habla a nivel mundial de lo que puede suceder. "Los modelos climáticos nos dicen que es probable que ciertas regiones superen esas temperaturas en los próximos 30 a 50 años. Las áreas más vulnerables incluyen el sur de Asia, el Golfo Pérsico y el Mar Rojo alrededor de 2050; y el este de China, partes del sudeste asiático y Brasil para 2070".

articles.title: Sea otters returned to a polluted California estuary in 1984; eelgrass expanded 600%, while marsh-edge erosion later slowed by 69% on average
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: When sea otters returned to California’s Elkhorn Slough in 1984, the estuary was already facing severe environmental pressure. The coastal wetland had.
articles.body: When sea otters returned to California’s Elkhorn Slough in 1984, the estuary was already facing severe environmental pressure. The coastal wetland had high nutrient levels linked to its agriculture-dominated watershed, while eelgrass had fallen to an all-time low of just 2 hectares.Decades later, researchers found that the return of the predators had effects far beyond their own population. Since sea otters recolonised the estuary, the extent of eelgrass beds increased by 600%. A later study also found that erosion of creek banks and marsh edges in areas with large otter populations slowed by an average of 69%.The two studies show how the recovery of a top predator can affect different parts of an ecosystem. The first study, published in PNAS in 2013, examined the relationship between sea otters, crabs, smaller grazers and eelgrass. The second, published in Nature in 2024, found that the effects extended to the physical stability of salt marshes.Elkhorn Slough is a highly nutrient-loaded estuary on California’s central coast. Nutrient concentrations increased sharply in the 1970s, and these changes were associated with a decline in eelgrass between 1965 and 1984. At the same time, nutrient loading in the watershed continued to increase.The return of sea otters changed this pattern through a trophic cascade, a chain of effects that begins with a predator and moves through several levels of the food web.How Sea Otters Helped EelgrassSea otters feed on crabs, which prey on smaller animals known as mesograzers. These include animals such as sea slugs and isopods. Mesograzers feed on algae growing on eelgrass.This algae, also called epiphytes, can cover eelgrass and reduce the light reaching its leaves. By eating crabs, sea otters indirectly allow more mesograzers to survive. These grazers then remove more algae from eelgrass.The 2013 study found that crabs made up 52% of the diet of sea otters feeding on or near eelgrass beds. Crabs of the Cancer genus alone accounted for 43% of their diet.After sea otters returned, crab biomass and size declined significantly. Researchers also found a strong relationship between sea otter predation on crabs and eelgrass expansion between 2006 and 2012.The pattern was also seen when researchers compared different parts of the ecosystem. Areas with more sea otters had fewer and smaller crabs, more large mesograzers, lower loads of algal epiphytes and greater eelgrass biomass.Experiments supported the same explanation. When researchers simulated low sea otter predation by using large crabs, more sea slugs died, algae increased and eelgrass lost biomass. When crab predation was reduced, mesograzers increased and eelgrass performed better.The findings were significant because nutrient pollution continued to affect the estuary. Despite these pressures, sea otter predation helped reduce one of the biological effects of nutrient loading and supported eelgrass growth.From Eelgrass To Marsh StabilityThe 2024 Nature study looked at another part of Elkhorn Slough- its salt marshes and creek edges. Researchers found that as sea otter numbers increased, erosion of marsh edges generally slowed, even as the ecosystem faced physical pressures including rising sea levels, stronger tidal currents and increased water flow from inland areas.The Elkhorn Slough Foundation said erosion of creek banks and marsh edges in areas with large otter populations slowed by an average of 69%.The researchers linked this change to the predators’ effect on marsh crabs. These crabs burrow into salt marsh soil and feed on marsh roots. Their activity can weaken the edges of marshes and contribute to erosion.“Crabs eat salt marsh roots, dig into salt marsh soil, and over time can cause a salt marsh to erode and collapse,” Brent Hughes, lead author of the study, said.“This had been happening at Elkhorn Slough for decades until sea otters recolonized the estuary in the mid-1980s,” he added. “After a few decades, in areas the sea otters had recolonized, salt marshes and creekbanks were becoming more stable again, despite rising sea levels, increased water flow from inland sources, and greater pollution.”Researchers conducted predator-exclusion experiments in five marsh creeks. These experiments showed that sea otters suppressed burrowing crabs, which increased marsh-edge strength and reduced erosion.A Predator With Wider EffectsTogether, the studies show that the return of sea otters affected both living organisms and the physical structure of the coastal ecosystem.The earlier research showed how the predator’s presence moved through the food web: fewer crabs meant more mesograzers, fewer algae on eelgrass and greater eelgrass growth.The later research found another chain of effects. Fewer marsh crabs meant less damage to marsh roots and soil, helping creek banks and marsh edges remain more stable.The researchers said the findings suggest that the loss of top predators can contribute to the decline of coastal wetlands, while restoring them may help re-establish ecosystem function and geomorphic stability.

articles.title: Underwater sensors caught a rare event off Cornwall: one porpoise became trapped in a net while two animals exchanged possible distress calls
articles.summary: Wildlife & Biodiversity News: Off the coast of Cornwall, a set of underwater sensors was listening to the ocean when it detected something researchers rarely get to see. According .
articles.body: Off the coast of Cornwall, a set of underwater sensors was listening to the ocean when it detected something researchers rarely get to see. According to an online report by Phys Org, two harbor porpoises swam around a fishing net, seemingly foraging for food and avoiding the gear, until one got caught up in it. What happened next was recorded in unusual detail, both acoustically and in terms of movement, providing researchers a rare insight into how these animals might react to a dangerous encounter. Scientists from the University of St Andrews’ Sea Mammal Research Unit and Scottish Oceans Institute found that their passive acoustic monitoring systems had inadvertently detected the bycatch event. Their results were published on August 26 in Royal Society Open Science. The devices had been deployed on a static gill net off Cornwall to detect marine mammal activity. Two harbor porpoises were observed foraging for several minutes around the gear and were recorded. The animals seemed to know how to avoid the net. Perhaps while chasing prey, one may have lost sight of the obstacle for a moment and became entangled, researchers speculate.Once caught, the porpoise could exert enough force to snap the net, but never enough to get away.Potential distress callsThese recordings offered more than evidence of the entanglement. The acoustic data showed that the two porpoises exchanged different types of calls during the incident. Researchers say some of the sounds may have been distress calls, but more study is needed to determine exactly what the calls conveyed. Together, the sound and movement data give scientists an unusually detailed view of an event that is normally difficult, if not impossible, to see in real time.The role of By-catchBycatch, the accidental capture of animals in fishing gear is considered the world’s greatest direct human-caused threat to dolphins and porpoises. It is believed that around 1,000 porpoises die each year after being caught in static fishing nets in the UK. However, recording such encounters is difficult due to the thousands of kilometers of fishing gear deployed across UK waters, only a fraction of which can be monitored. “The chances of sensors recording a bycatch event at the exact moment are very slim,” said lead researcher Dr Jamie Macaulay. “Finding out how and why entanglements happen could lead to practical solutions for researchers and the fishing industry,” he said.For safer fishing equipmentThe findings could help lead to new methods of reducing accidental captures. Researchers are looking at options such as more acoustically reflective nets so that marine mammals can detect fishing gear more easily, nets that allow stronger animals to escape, and biomimetic acoustic deterrents designed to warn animals away. The researchers stress that the goal is not necessarily to stop static-net fishing, which is still important to the fishing industry, but to make it safer. Scientists are hoping partnerships with fishing communities, such as the UK Bycatch Monitoring Program and CIBBRiNA, will allow them to turn rare glimpses beneath the waves into solutions that can save marine mammals.

articles.title: A seagrass meadow was transplanted off an Italian island in 2009; 17 years later, scientists found signs of a functioning ecosystem
articles.summary: Nature & Environment News: A seagrass meadow transplanted off the Italian island of Ischia in 2009 is offering evidence of what restoration can look like over the long term. 17 .
articles.body: A seagrass meadow transplanted off the Italian island of Ischia in 2009 is offering evidence of what restoration can look like over the long term. 17 years later, scientists have returned to the site and found encouraging signs that parts of the restored Posidonia oceanica meadow are developing into a functioning ecosystem. The latest monitoring campaign suggests that successful restoration is about more than keeping transplanted plants alive. A restored meadow may gradually regain ecological functions. The findings are valuable because long-term monitoring of Mediterranean seagrass restoration remains uncommon, leaving major questions about what happens after the first few years of a project.Story of Ischia seagrass meadow that was transplanted off the Italian islandThe meadow was transplanted in 2009 in the waters of the Regno di Nettuno Marine Protected Area, off Ischia. In May 2026, researchers from ISPRA, Italy's national environmental research and protection institute, returned to the site as part of the Interreg Euro-MED ARTEMIS project.According to the ARTEMIS report, the researchers examined different restored areas because the transplanted sections had not all experienced the same level of success. They also compared the restored plots with nearby natural Posidonia oceanica meadows, allowing them to assess how the transplanted habitat had changed over nearly two decades.That long period is one of the most important parts of the story. Many restoration projects are assessed soon after transplantation, but Posidonia meadows develop slowly. A project that appears promising after a few years may still need much more time before scientists can understand whether it is genuinely recovering as an ecosystem.The Ischia site therefore provides an unusually long view of the process. The 2026 campaign was designed to look beyond the condition of the plants themselves and examine whether the restored meadow was beginning to perform the wider ecological roles expected from a healthy seagrass habitat.Ischia seagrass meadow becoming a functioning ecosystem over 17 yearsThe researchers studied both the physical and functional characteristics of the restored seagrass and the biodiversity associated with it. According to ARTEMIS, the results were encouraging in the areas where the transplanted shoots had successfully established.Tiziano Bacci, a marine biologist and researcher at ISPRA, said many ecological indicators in those successful areas were now comparable to those found in nearby natural Posidonia oceanica meadows. Some differences remain and are still being investigated, but the findings suggest that a carefully restored meadow can gradually recover important elements of its original ecological character.This distinction matters because a restoration project cannot be judged simply by counting surviving plants. A meadow becomes more meaningful when it also begins supporting the relationships and processes that make the habitat useful to the wider marine environment.The ARTEMIS report says the Ischia findings show signs of recovery in the meadow's structure, functions and ecosystem services. In practical terms, this means the restored habitat is beginning to resemble a living system rather than merely a collection of surviving transplanted shoots.A healthy meadow can support life above and below the seabedPosidonia oceanica is one of the Mediterranean's most important seagrass species. Its meadows provide habitat for marine biodiversity, help protect coastlines and store carbon.The ARTEMIS project, which focuses on restoring and conserving Mediterranean seagrass meadows, describes these habitats as valuable parts of the region's natural infrastructure. The project works on restoration methods while also exploring ways to incorporate the benefits of seagrass ecosystems into policy and investment decisions.At Ischia, the long-term results suggest that restored seagrass can eventually provide many of these benefits again when conditions allow. ARTEMIS notes that a recovering meadow can support marine life, contribute to coastal protection, store carbon and improve the resilience of the surrounding ecosystem.However, the story does not suggest that transplantation offers a quick or automatic solution. The difference between the various restored areas at Ischia shows that success can vary within the same project. Environmental conditions and the ability of transplanted shoots to establish themselves can make a major difference to the eventual outcome.Long-term monitoring is essential for seagrass restorationBarbara La Porta, a senior researcher at ISPRA, said the Ischia case demonstrates why restoration sites need to be monitored over long periods. According to ARTEMIS, long-term data from Mediterranean seagrass restoration projects remain scarce, even though such information is needed to improve techniques and guide future work.The monitoring at Ischia can help scientists understand how restored meadows evolve over time. That knowledge may improve restoration methods, refine the way projects are assessed and make it easier to distinguish between short-term survival and genuine ecological recovery. The Ischia meadow is especially useful because it offers something that newer projects cannot yet provide, which is evidence gathered after 17 years.Mediterranean restoration still faces funding and coordination problemsThe encouraging results from Ischia come at a time when Mediterranean seagrass restoration is facing much larger challenges. Oceanographic Magazine reports that restoration efforts across the region remain too small, isolated and poorly funded to reverse the continuing decline of Posidonia oceanica at the necessary scale.The report highlighted pressures including coastal development, anchoring damage and climate change. It also found that restoration is often hindered by inconsistent governance, differing technical standards and funding that does not match the long timescales required for ecosystems to recover.The Ischia case gives a real-world example of why patience matters. Seventeen years is a long time to wait for evidence, but that is precisely what makes the meadow valuable as a case study.The transplanted seagrass off Ischia has not simply produced a story of plants that survived. In its most successful areas, scientists are now seeing signs of an ecosystem that is beginning to function in ways comparable to a natural Posidonia meadow. The lesson is not that every restoration project will achieve the same result, but that lasting recovery can require careful planning, suitable conditions and, above all, time.
